title: Cap. III Rat. 5: foresight election would be acceptor personarum
latin: Rat. 5. Si Deus ex meritis praevisis eligeret quosdam ad gloriam, aliis praeteritis, esset acceptor personarum. Nam electio justa et rationabilis disparitatem quandam inter electos et non-electos praesupponit; et prudens semper quod est melius eligit. Cum ergo nulla excogitari possit differentia inter homines absque hac praevisione meritorum in aliquibus, quae non praevidentur in aliis, consequens est ut dicamus, electionem Dei semper inniti hujusmodi praescientiae humanorum meritorum.
pass_a: Reason 5. If God from foreseen merits should elect certain ones to glory, others being passed by, he would be an acceptor of persons. For a just and rational election presupposes a certain disparity between the elect and the non-elect; and the prudent always elects what is better. Since therefore no difference can be thought up between men apart from this foresight of merits in some, which are not foreseen in others, it follows that we should say that God's election always rests on this sort of foresight of human merits.
pass_b: Rat. 5. If God elected some to glory from foresight of merits and passed others by, he would be an acceptor of persons. A just, rational election presupposes some disparity between elect and non-elect, and the prudent always chooses what is better. Since no difference among people can be imagined apart from foresight of merits in some that are not foreseen in others, it follows that God's election always rests on that kind of foresight of human merits.

lemmas.gloss: elect some from foresight; pass others

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 5: Pelagian/Faustus charge; Bannes — can elect equal or worse
latin: Sol. Hoc argumentum ab antiquis Pelagianis urgeri solitum, patet ex Augustino multis in locis: Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 7. Et epist. 105. ad Sixtum, Hypogn. contra Pelag. lib. 6. et alibi. Quinetiam antesignanus Semipelagianorum Faustus Regiensis sic argumentatur lib. 2. cap. 4. Si ambo res sunt in natura, in isto justitia periclitabitur, qui sine merito indignus eligitur. Sed respondemus cum doctissimo Bannesio, Deum posse absque ulla injustitia, aut vitiosa personarum acceptione non modo ex duobus hominibus prorsus aequalibus unum eligere ad vitam aeternam, alio praeterito, sed etiam illum eligere quem praescivit pluribus et gravioribus peccatis implicandum, illo relicto quem praevidit pauciora et leviora admissurum, In 1. quest. 23. art. 5.
pass_a: Solution. That this argument was wont to be pressed by the ancient Pelagians is clear from Augustine in many places: Against the two Epistles of the Pelagians book 2 chapter 7. And epistle 105 to Sixtus, Hypognosticon against the Pelagians book 6, and elsewhere. Moreover the standard-bearer of the Semipelagians, Faustus of Riez, argues thus in book 2 chapter 4: If both are equal in nature, justice is endangered in that one who is elected unworthy without merit. But we answer with the most learned Banez, that God can without any injustice, or vicious acceptation of persons, not only from two men altogether equal elect one to eternal life, the other being passed by, but even elect him whom he foresaw would be entangled in more and heavier sins, leaving him whom he foresaw would admit fewer and lighter ones, On 1. q. 23 art. 5.
pass_b: Sol. This argument was the old Pelagian press — Augustine shows it in many places (Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. 2.7; Ep. 105 to Sixtus; Hypogn. contra Pelag. 6; and elsewhere). Even Faustus of Riez, champion of the Semipelagians, argues (lib. 2.4): if both are equal in nature, justice is at risk when the one without merit is elected unworthy. We answer with Banez: without injustice or vicious respect of persons God can not only elect one of two wholly equal people to eternal life and pass the other by, but even elect the one he foresaw would be entangled in more and heavier sins, leaving the one he foresaw would commit fewer and lighter (In 1. q. 23 art. 5).

lemmas.gloss: Banez: no injustice in unequal election
may elect equal or the worse sinner

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 5: loving and electing make worthier; Colossians 1:12
latin: Hujus autem rei hanc rationem afferre licet, Quia Deus diligendo et eligendo facit eos digniores et meliores, quos diligit et eligit. Humana electio, quae facere non potest disparitatem dignitatis in rebus electis, tenetur tendere in illud objectum in quo praesupponitur major dignitas: sed ad Divinae electionis justitiam et sapientiam statuendam sufficit quod cum omnes homines sint indignissimi hoc electionis beneficio, Deus eligendo facit illos quos ad gloriam eligit prae aliis dignos et idoneos ad participandam sortem sanctorum in lumine, Coloss. i. 12.
pass_a: But of this matter this reason may be brought, Because God by loving and electing makes those worthier and better whom he loves and elects. Human election, which cannot make a disparity of dignity in the things elected, is bound to tend to that object in which a greater dignity is presupposed: but to establish the justice and wisdom of the divine election it suffices that, since all men are most unworthy of this benefit of election, God by electing makes those whom he elects to glory before others worthy and fit to share the lot of the saints in light, Colossians 1:12.
pass_b: The reason: by loving and electing, God makes those he loves and elects worthier and better. Human choice cannot create disparity of worth in what it chooses, so it must aim at the object where greater dignity is already assumed. For divine election's justice and wisdom it is enough that, though all people are most unworthy of this electing gift, God by electing makes those he elects to glory fit and worthy ahead of others to share the saints' lot in light (Colossians 1:12).

lemmas.gloss: fit for the saints' lot in light

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 5: Thomas and Augustine — electing makes worthy; holy not foreseen
latin: Hoc Thomas annotavit, Necesse est dicere quod Deus quosdam aliis magis amet. Nam cum amor Dei sit causa bonitatis rerum, non esset aliquid alio melius, si Deus non vellet uni majus bonum quam alteri. Part. I. qu. 20. art. 3. Et in commentariis ad Rom. cap. 9. Electio non respicit bonum in homine, sed facit. Quod ab Augustino didicit, qui contra Jul. Pelag. lib. 5. cap. 3. docet, Deum non elegisse quos praevidit dignos, sed eligendo effecisse dignos. Uterque hanc doctrinam hausit ab Apostolo, qui dicit, Deum elegisse nos ut sancti essemus; non quia sancti praevisi fuimus.
pass_a: This Thomas noted: It is necessary to say that God loves some more than others. For since the love of God is the cause of the goodness of things, there would not be something better than another, if God did not will a greater good to one than to another. Part I q. 20 art. 3. And in the commentaries on Romans chapter 9: Election does not look to a good in the human being, but makes it. Which he learned from Augustine, who against Julian the Pelagian book 5 chapter 3 teaches that God did not elect those whom he foresaw worthy, but by electing made them worthy. Both drew this doctrine from the Apostle, who says that God elected us that we should be holy; not because we were foreseen holy.
pass_b: Thomas notes: we must say God loves some more than others — for God's love is the cause of things' goodness, and nothing would be better than another if he did not will a greater good to one than to another (ST I q.20 a.3). On Romans 9: election does not look to a good already in the person but makes it. He learned that from Augustine (Contra Jul. Pelag. 5.3): God did not elect those he foresaw as worthy, but by electing made them worthy. Both drew it from the Apostle: God elected us that we should be holy — not because we were foreseen holy.

lemmas.gloss: election makes the good it regards
elected to be holy, not as foreseen holy

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 5 close: unjust acceptio vs liberal gift; Matthew 20:15
latin: Ad haec; injusta personarum acceptio locum non habet, ubi quis ex mera liberalitate de suo dat inaequaliter aequalibus, sed ubi, in dispensatione rerum debitarum, quis uni faveat prae altero, ex respectu ad aliquam personae circumstantiam quae est extra causam meriti: ut si Praelatus in collatione beneficii praeferat divitem aut consanguineum suum doctoribus et melioribus viris, est personarum acceptor, quia respicit circumstantias, quae nihil faciunt ad meritum vel dignitatem talis praemii. Jam vero Deus eligens ad regnum gloriae unum prae alio, non agit ex debito justitiae, sed ex dono munificentiae: neque respicit nobilitatem, divitias, ingenium, aut aliam qualitatem quamcunque extra rem, unde personarum nomen invenit; sed liberalitatem et bonitatem suam, juxta illud, Matth. xx. 15. Licet mihi quod volo facere de eo. Videte Augustinum, Epist. 106. et De bono persever. lib. 2. cap. 8. Et contr. 2. Epist. Pelag. cap. 3. lib. 2.
pass_a: To these things; unjust acceptation of persons has no place where someone from mere liberality of his own gives unequally to equals, but where, in the dispensing of things owed, someone favors one before another from regard to some circumstance of the person which is outside the cause of merit: as if a Prelate in the conferring of a benefice should prefer a rich man or his kinsman to more learned and better men, he is an acceptor of persons, because he regards circumstances which do nothing toward the merit or dignity of such a prize. But now God electing one to the kingdom of glory before another does not act from a debt of justice, but from a gift of munificence: nor does he regard nobility, riches, talent, or any other quality whatever outside the matter from which the name of persons is found; but his liberality and goodness, according to that, Matthew 20:15. Is it lawful for me to do what I will with my own? See Augustine, Epistle 106, and On the Good of Perseverance book 2 chapter 8. And against the two Epistles of the Pelagians chapter 3 book 2.
pass_b: Further: unjust respect of persons has no place where someone from mere liberality gives unequally of what is his own to equals — only where, in dispensing what is owed, he favors one over another for a personal circumstance outside the cause of merit (as when a prelate, conferring a benefice, prefers a rich man or kinsman to better and more learned men: that is respect of persons, because those circumstances do nothing for the merit or dignity of such a prize). God electing one to the kingdom of glory ahead of another does not act from a debt of justice but from a gift of munificence; he does not regard nobility, riches, talent, or any quality outside the matter that earns the name "respect of persons," but his own liberality and goodness — Matthew 20:15: Is it lawful for me to do what I will with my own? See Augustine, Ep. 106; De bono persever. 2.8; Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. 2.3.

lemmas.gloss: no unjust respect in free gifts
glory not owed justice but gift
lawful to do what I will with my own
